story_text.value:
Hi HN! I built Groundtrack to help coding agents continuously learn and improve from their work across a company.

With coding agents handling most of code implementation, a lot of things like review corrections, failed approaches, and discovered constraints stay trapped in individual agent sessions, so future agents can repeat the same failures. Sometimes a broken or agent-unfriendly tool or workflow can cause those issues too; if multiple agents independently find workarounds, those failures don’t get connected and aren’t used to improve the system around the agents.

Groundtrack turns those learnings into scoped and shared engineering experiences that can help future agents across teams working with Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, and OpenCode. It retrieves relevant lessons during later work, records whether they helped, and updates or supersedes knowledge as it learns over time.

It also identifies recurring friction that shouldn’t just become another stored experience. If agents repeatedly struggle with the same tool or workflow, Groundtrack creates an evidence-backed draft initiative so the team can fix the underlying environment and prevent a certain class of mistake systemically.

For example, on the landing page, I follow a database migration incident through the entire loop. Groundtrack turned the original workaround into a scoped experience, surfaced it when a later agent encountered similar migration drift, and recorded that it was successfully applied. After connecting evidence from seven sessions, it also proposed making the safe migration workflow a permanent part of the engineering environment and prevent the issue altogether.

There have been many challenges I’ve already run into to make this helpful (and still many unsolved things!), one of which has been generalizing and determining the applicability of one lesson to another session. I wrote about some of my retrieval experiments here: https://groundtrack.dev/blog/retrieving-knowledge-that-appli...

It’s an early product and I’d really love any and all feedback I can get. If you or your team regularly use coding agents, please try it on an active project and see if it helps your agents learn and improve over time. It’s free for solo use.

title.value: Show HN: Groundtrack – Continual learning for coding agents

story_text.value:
The Obsidian forum has threads reporting Sync data loss for over 2 years. To help reproduce bugs, I built a fuzzer that runs Obsidian instances in containers, makes them edit notes while cutting off their network, and documents the failure rates.

The fuzzer finds amusingly short sequences that cause data loss and that you can reproduce on your own in a minute (if you have an Obsidian Sync subscription). Steps in the repro README.

I guided Claude Code to build the fuzzer, but I didn't read the code. This didn't go well. The project ballooned to a painful 60h, so I wrote a separate experience report on the many failure modes and what I'll do differently next time: https://hmijail.substack.com/p/building-a-semantic-fuzzer-fo...

story_text.value:
I lived with Anxiety Disorders (and Panic Attack, avoidance behavior) from 27 to 37 years old, at first I saw my general practionner who refer me to psychiatrist who listen to me 15 minutes and prescribe me anxiety pills

Where I come from (France), official data show 13% of population takes pills for anxiety, and I didn't want for personal reason increase that statistic.

Unfortunately, at that time (now I'm 44), all informations on the topic was very fragmented, and ultimately the self discovery journey to understand my trigger, find peace, and take control of my anxiety took way too much time.

For me Anxiety and avoidance behavior result in staying way too long in situation I should have avoided (relationship, business)

But in this journey, I also meet incredible therapist, daily relaxation method, and technique for self discovery that I accept it as part of a cool life journey.

4 years ago I decided I want to share this, first with a book (that I sold to 45 people ) and a Checklist (yes... not the right format, I was just replicating my other business "SEO Checklist") while building my content Hub, the Anxiety University, that grew from 0 to 78 human made article

Then I decided to invest into my own CBT Training Program and first hypnotherapy session but lost all money because the therapists I hired got cancer (and the other one hide the situation to burn my 30k invest to produce it)

I then pivot to a full fledge mobile app, without AI (more on that later) and cut a deal with a Neuro Psychologist in NY and Panic Expert in Australia to license their course. But the bundle inside the app looked too much as a "Upsell Money Grab" so I eventually shut this down recently.

3 Years later, Anxiety Checklist is DR70 and thanks to AI and Claude Code, I finally have a good app with proper tracking and can use data to improve my onboarding, understand better my audience, and itterate 10x faster (and cheaper) but with strong old school human made fondation.

Today I'm launching on Product Hunt with new onboarding showing 7% download to free trial conversion rate, and hope that I'll finally have something I can scale with ads.

For me it's not just about the money, I really like this mission, but as any business, I need the economic to make sense to add more content, hire more talent, and marketing to get more exposure.

Anyhow, the journey was fun, even though I burned 225k USD in this venture over 3 years... I called it my money pitt :))

My plan if paid aquisition fail is to put everything free and launch a therapist directory (the app is in complement of therapy, not a replacement)

3 Years, multiple pivot, still not profitable, that's my lame story, but still not giving up.

title.value: Show HN: Anxiety Checklist – 3 years of itterate with no success yet

story_text.value:
One topic I've been researching lately is the best way to handle switching to another agent when I hit a usage limit on one of them. For example, if I hit the usage limit on Codex, I would want to switch to Claude Code and vice versa.

The important part is not losing the ongoing context/task(s) when switching between the tools.. I have found a few things that say they do this but none seem to have much traction.

As a result, I was hoping to pick the brain of HN'ers to see how you all handle this

(To head off comments regarding 'pay for a better plan for more usage' - I can't currently really afford the jump from $20 a month per agent to $100-200/m per agent)

title.value: Ask HN: How do you handle hitting AI coding agent usage limits?

story_text.value:
Hey everyone, SideKernel is the result of my capstone project for my MSc at Georgia Tech.

There are a lot of sandboxes on the market right now for AI agents, but most of them focus on production deployments, rather than coding agents (e.g. Claude Code).

I always felt uncomfortable running Claude Code or other coding agents directly on my machine, and I didn't want to buy a second computer or rent a VPS just for that.

That's why I made SideKernel: a sandbox that tries to be as transparent as possible to the everyday developer.

I hope you find some value in it, and feedback is more than welcome. Usability is hard to get right without large user studies, so I'd really value hearing about any annoyances or blockers you run into.

Thanks!

story_text.value:
Hey there! We are building SuperCMO Skills, open source tools which allow agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, etc.) to research, plan and create video and image campaigns end-to-end right out of your terminal or IDE.

We got tired of paying for expensive AI subscriptions and wasting countless hours assembling a pipeline for just one video ad, so we created these tools for ourselves. SuperCMO integrates with your agents to provide the ability to plan, shoot, edit, and stitch complete campaigns.

We began with simple prompt wrappers but soon realized the need to rethink our entire pipeline to overcome common limitations of the AI video.

- Pipeline Orchestration: Creating one ad now requires jumping through several apps: writing scripts in one, creating images in another, recording audio in yet another, and stitching the whole thing in an editor. SuperCMO does all of that natively. The tool knows how to choose the appropriate model (like automatically switching prompts for Veo versus Seedance) and do the whole post-production, including trimming and voiceover synchronization.

- Consistency from Shot to Shot: In true AI video generators, products and actors continually transform from shot to shot. We solved that problem by storyboarding before rendering and locking in master reference images in every generation.

- Directional Control: Completely automated agents often go awry creatively. So, we've developed the capabilities to take a peek at every stage of the process. You're always in control, approving the creator, the story idea, and the script before anything is expensively rendered.

People are using this today to create UGC product ads (give the agent a product photo and it chooses the creator, generates the script, and creates a ready MP4 file) or to analyze competitors' work (agent analyzes the winning advertisement from the competitor and recreates it with your product in mind).

This project will be released under an Apache-2.0 license. You can come to us with your own vendor keys to have everything done for free or to generate using our keys and just pay for each usage without any lock-in.

Thank you for your attention!

story_text.value:
Hello, Caffold is an open-source, self-hosted workspace for coding agents. You can continue the same work across desktop, foldable, tablet, and phone.

I started building it for myself in late June. It was initially only for Codex. I got a Galaxy Z Fold8 in early August and started using Caffold much more seriously. By late August, I had moved my existing Codex work into Caffold too. I've been doing all of my development work in Caffold since then. After about a month of that, it finally feels ready to share. For now, it supports the three agents I actually use day to day: Codex, Claude Code, and Grok.

The idea came from how my work had changed. Coding agents now write almost all of the code. I spend most of my time reading code and diffs, watching what the agents are doing, steer them when needed, and give the next instruction.

When I saw the upcoming Fold8, its unfolded screen looked large enough for this kind of work. I rarely need to type code myself. I often enter prompts by voice as well as with a keyboard. So I started wondering if a foldable could be my main interface for development rather than just a secondary device.

I also wanted to see how far I could go with the browser platform itself. The frontend is plain JavaScript and CSS. It uses Web Components and native ES modules. There is no TypeScript, React/Vue/Svelte, or bundler. (That doesn't mean I avoid external libraries entirely. I use things like xterm.js and pdf.js where they make sense.)

I'm also curious how many people will want to use foldables this way, especially now that devices like the iPhone Duo are coming too.

story_text.value:
I built TalkToMe, an open-source macOS app that lets an agent call you from its current session. You answer, talk, and hear its replies. The agent keeps its tools, files, and history.

It works with Codex (Tested extensively, quite smooth), Claude Code (not tested heavily), Hermes, and other agents that can run shell commands. You can use ElevenLabs or local models to power the conversation. It's really surreal to see your agent call you for something!

title.value: Show HN: Talktome - let your AI Agent call you
